title: Why so high?
teaches: Wavelength against the size of an insect, why higher calls find smaller prey but carry less far, and the two shapes of call: sweeps and steady tones
summary: **Sound is a wave of squeezed and stretched air.** It travels at about 343 metres a second, and its wavelength is that speed divided by the frequency.
**Bat calls have short waves.** At 20 kHz a wave is 17 mm long, at 50 kHz 7 mm, and at 100 kHz 3.4 mm.
**Small targets hardly echo long waves.** Once an insect is much smaller than the wavelength, its echo fades steeply, so a bat hunting midges does best calling high.
**Air soaks up high sound.** About half a decibel a metre at 20 kHz, three or more at 100 kHz, so a high call does not reach far.
**Every bat strikes a bargain.** Big brown and hoary bats call low, near 20 to 28 kHz, for long range in open air; Yuma myotis call near 50 kHz for small insects close by.
**Bats shout.** A call is 120 to 140 decibels at 10 cm from the mouth, as loud as a jet engine nearby, and silent to us.
**Sweeps measure.** A short sweep down through many frequencies, 1 to 10 ms long, gives sharp timing and detail; every Washington bat uses them.
**Steady tones catch wingbeats.** A horseshoe bat holds one pitch for 30 to 60 ms, calling most of the time, and hears the flicker of an insect's wings in the echo.

blocks.text: On a summer evening over a street in Seattle, a big brown bat flies along the line of the treetops. Its calls start near 50 kilohertz and sweep down to about 25, ten or so a second. Seven thousand kilometres away, over a hedge in southern England, a greater horseshoe bat hangs from a twig and turns about, calling through its nose on a single steady note of 83 kilohertz. Both are hunting insects. Neither call can be heard by a person standing underneath.

The first lesson ended with the bat listening to echoes of its own calls, and those calls are far higher than they seem to need to be. A bat could call at 2 kilohertz, a sharp whistle anyone can hear, and the echoes would come back off walls and trees just as well; people find their way along a dark corridor by the echo of their own footsteps. Yet hardly any bat that hunts insects calls below about 10 kilohertz, and most call far higher. Before reading on, think about what an insect a few millimetres long might do to a sound.

A sound is air being squeezed and stretched. A bat's larynx, like ours, pushes on the air in front of it and pulls back, many thousands of times a second, and each push packs the air a little tighter before it passes the squeeze on to the air beyond. The squeezes travel outward at the **speed of sound**, about 343 metres a second in air at 20 °C, while the air itself only shivers back and forth.[^speed]

The distance from one squeeze to the next is the **wavelength**. A sound of frequency *f* sends out *f* squeezes each second. By the end of that second the first squeeze is 343 metres away, so the *f* squeezes are spread over 343 metres, each 343 ÷ *f* metres behind the one before. A deep note of 100 hertz has waves 3.4 metres long. A whistle at 2 kilohertz has waves 17 cm long, a little shorter than a pencil. At 20 kilohertz the waves are 17 mm long, at 50 kilohertz 7 mm, and at 100 kilohertz 3.4 mm, the length of a sesame seed.

A wave meeting something much bigger than itself bounces back, as sea waves bounce off a harbour wall. A wave meeting something much smaller hardly notices it: sea waves roll past a mooring post and close up behind it, and only a faint ripple spreads back from the post. Sound behaves the same way. A wall echoes any pitch. A midge 3 mm long, met by a 20 kilohertz call with waves 17 mm long, is a mooring post in a swell.

blocks.task: Find a pitch at which the midge echoes strongly

blocks.text: The fall-off is steep. Once a target is well below the wavelength in size, halving its size cuts the power of its echo to about a sixty-fourth, and doubling the wavelength cuts it to a sixteenth.[^rayleigh] Once the insect is about as big as the wavelength or bigger, raising the pitch further adds little to its echo. So a bat that calls high gets echoes from small insects that a low-calling bat would barely notice, and since a moth's wings are several centimetres across, even the lowest-calling bats get a strong echo from a moth.

For small prey short waves would seem the better choice, yet many bats call low, because air soaks up sound. Each squeeze heats the air very slightly, and that heat is lost from the wave; a high sound makes more squeezes in each metre it travels, so it loses more on the way. Sound fades as it spreads out in any case, but on top of that the air itself soaks up high sound quickly. Loudness is counted in **decibels** (dB), from 0 near the faintest sound a young person can hear, through about 60 for conversation, with each 10 dB a tenfold change in power.[^decibel] At 20 kilohertz, air at room temperature soaks up about half a decibel for each metre the sound travels. At 50 kilohertz it takes 1.5 to 2 decibels a metre, and at 100 kilohertz 3 or more.

An echo has to go out and come back, so it pays twice. To a target 10 metres away and back, a 20 kilohertz call loses about 10 decibels to the air, a tenth of its power. A 100 kilohertz call loses about 66 decibels, leaving a few ten-millionths. To make up for all this, bats call very loudly: 120 to 140 decibels measured 10 cm from the mouth, as loud as a jet engine heard from nearby. A bat tightens small muscles in its middle ear at the instant it calls, damping its own hearing so as not to deafen itself.

blocks.caption: How far away a bat can hear a midge (dashed) and a moth (solid), by the pitch of its call. A model: the call is 130 dB at 10 cm, the bat detects echoes down to 20 dB, and each insect is treated as a small ball, a simplification.

blocks.text: No pitch does everything. A low call carries to a moth 10 metres off, but finds a midge only when it is too close to catch; a high call finds the midge, but the air swallows it before it gets far. Each kind of bat strikes its own bargain. Big brown and hoary bats, which hunt moths and beetles in open air, call low, putting most of each call's energy near 20 to 28 kilohertz, and can hear a big insect many metres off. The Yuma myotis, which skims the water of Seattle's lakes for midges and caddisflies, calls near 50 kilohertz and works close in. The horseshoe bats of the Old World, calling at 80 kilohertz and above, hunt among leaves at a few metres' range.

blocks.text: Pitch is not the whole story; a call also has a shape. The easiest way to see one is a **sonogram**, a picture of sound with time running across and pitch running up, so that a note held steady is a level line and a sweep is a slope. Bat calls come in two broad shapes.

Most bats, and every bat in Washington, make **FM** calls, for frequency modulated: short sweeps from high to low, each 1 to 10 milliseconds long, a few to a dozen a second while searching, with long silences between. A sweep crosses many frequencies in a few thousandths of a second, so its echo is sharp in time and carries detail: each part of the target echoes some frequencies more than others, and the bat can hear the difference between a leaf and a moth. The next lesson follows how a bat uses that sharp timing to judge distance.

Horseshoe bats, and a few other families, make **CF** calls, for constant frequency: a long steady tone, 30 to 60 milliseconds, with a short sweep at the end. They call most of the time they fly, with short gaps. A long steady note is poor for timing, but it is very good for one thing. When a flying insect is caught in the beam, its wings flash toward the bat on every beat, like a mirror turned in the sun, and each flash puts a bright **glint** in the echo. The glints come at the rate the wings beat, so a long echo holds several, evenly spaced, and the bat can hear the beat of a wing among the motionless leaves around it.[^horseshoe]

blocks.caption: Sonograms of the search calls (violet) of a big brown bat, a Yuma myotis and a greater horseshoe bat, with the echo from a moth a metre away (teal, dashed) and that echo's loudness below. The calls are synthesised from published measurements and slowed ten times when played, as a bat detector does, so a 50 kHz call is heard at 5 kHz.

blocks.text: Finding things by their echoes is called **sonar** when it uses sound, as ships and dolphins do under water,[^dolphins] and **radar** when it uses radio waves. Bats are often said to have radar, but their sound moves nearly a million times slower than radio waves, which is part of what makes the bat's problem possible: the delays it has to time are thousandths of a second, not millionths. Nor does a bat hold a picture of the world the way a screen does. Each call brings back a handful of echoes, and the bat builds its sense of what is ahead from many calls, one after another, as the next lessons show.

A few bats call low enough to be heard. The spotted bat of eastern Washington's canyons calls near 10 kilohertz, a plain high tick to anyone listening. The hoary bat's lowest notes, near 18 or 20 kilohertz, are at the top of a young person's hearing, and on a still evening in late summer some people can hear one pass. For the rest, a **bat detector** turns the calls into sounds we can hear; an optional lesson later in the course builds one.

blocks.caption: Five questions on why bats call so high
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A bat raises its call from 25 kHz to 50 kHz. What happens to the wavelength?
choices: It halves, from about 14 mm to about 7 mm
It doubles, from about 7 mm to about 14 mm
It stays the same, since the speed of sound does not change
items.why: Wavelength is the speed of sound divided by the frequency: 343 m/s divided by 25,000 is about 14 mm, and by 50,000 about 7 mm. Twice the frequency gives half the wavelength.

items.ask: Why does a bat calling at 20 kHz have trouble finding a midge 3 mm long?
choices: The waves, 17 mm long, mostly pass around the midge and return a very weak echo
The air soaks up 20 kHz sound too fast for any echo to come back
A 20 kHz call is too quiet for the bat to hear its echo at all
items.why: A target much smaller than the wavelength barely disturbs the wave, and its echo falls off steeply as it shrinks. Low calls carry far in air, which is why big brown bats use them for larger prey.

items.ask: Bats that hunt big moths in open air tend to call lower than bats that hunt midges near the water. Which explanation is best?
choices: Moths echo well even at long wavelengths, and low calls carry farther, so the bat can find prey at a distance
Low calls travel faster through air, so the echo from a distant moth comes back sooner
Low calls are louder for the same effort, and big prey needs a louder call to be heard at all
items.why: A moth's wings are several centimetres across, longer than the waves of any bat call, so it echoes at any pitch. All pitches travel at the same speed. A low call loses less to the air, giving the moth hunter range; the midge hunter needs short waves and works close in.

items.ask: A horseshoe bat calls on one steady pitch for about 50 ms. What does that long call let it do that a short sweep does not?
choices: Hear the regular glints from a flying insect's beating wings
Time the echo more precisely, to find the distance to the nearest centimetre
Reach farther, since a steady tone is not absorbed by the air
items.why: A long echo lasts through several wingbeats, and each beat flashes a glint. Sweeps are the better tool for timing; a steady tone loses energy to the air like any other sound of its pitch.

items.ask: Why is it misleading to say that bats find their way by radar?
choices: Radar uses radio waves, while bats use sound, which travels nearly a million times slower
Radar works only over water, while bats echolocate over land
Radar uses echoes, while bats sense the air pushed back from objects
items.why: Finding things by echoes of sound is sonar. The slowness of sound is part of what makes a bat's problem workable, with echoes that return in thousandths of a second.

speed.title: Speed of sound
speed.text: Sound travels faster in warm air: about 331 metres a second at 0 °C, plus 0.6 for each degree warmer, so 343 at 20 °C. Over a summer lake at dusk it is close to 343.

rayleigh.title: Rayleigh scattering
rayleigh.text: For a target much smaller than the wavelength, the power it scatters goes as its size to the sixth power divided by the wavelength to the fourth. Lord Rayleigh worked it out for light in 1871; the same rule makes the sky blue.

decibel.title: Decibels
decibel.text: Sound levels are counted in decibels above the faintest sound a young person can hear. A quiet room is about 30 dB, conversation 60, a jet engine nearby about 130. Ten decibels more is ten times the power; 20 is a hundred times; 60 is a million.

horseshoe.title: Calling through the nose
horseshoe.text: Horseshoe bats call through their nostrils, and the horseshoe-shaped flap of skin round them, the noseleaf, works like a megaphone, focusing the call into a beam. Their ears are tuned to a very narrow band round their own call, which a later lesson returns to.

dolphins.title: Other echolocators
dolphins.text: Dolphins and toothed whales echolocate under water with clicks, a few cave-nesting birds (the oilbird and some swiftlets) with audible clicks in dark caves, and some blind people with tongue clicks, finding walls, cars and trees by the echo.
